prompt.context: Our client is A+Airline Co., the third largest airline in the United States by passengers carried. This week, we have been flying on our primary competitor, Gamma Airline, and we noticed something interesting: they stopped accepting cash for in-flight food and beverage services and they now only accept major credit cards.
prompt.question: The CEO of A+Airline Co. wants to know: why did Gamma Airline switch from a Cash & Card system to a Credit Card only system, and should we follow them?

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of passengers have a credit card available?
clarifying_info.a: Roughly 99% of all consumers purchase their airline tickets using a credit card, so effectively all passengers on the plane have a credit card available to them.

clarifying_info.q: What items are sold on A+Airline flights?
clarifying_info.a: Only food and alcoholic beverage items are sold on A+Airline flights.

clarifying_info.q: Is this decision for domestic flights only or also international?
clarifying_info.a: This is a US domestic decision only. Ignore international.

clarifying_info.q: Have other airlines made the switch to card-only?
clarifying_info.a: Gamma is the only airline that has made the switch so far; however, all other airlines are evaluating the switch.

clarifying_info.q: How do Gamma and A+Airline compare?
clarifying_info.a: For the purposes of this case, Gamma and A+Airline should be considered exactly the same in all regards.

exhibits.title: An Average A+Airline Flight
exhibits.shows: Seat configuration and passenger data for a typical A+Airline Boeing 737-800: total seats, class breakdown, load factors, business vs. leisure split, purchase rates, average spend per passenger type, and current share of in-flight purchases made by cash vs. credit card.

data.note: First Class passengers receive free food & beverage

exhibits.title: A+Airline Cash & Card Operations
exhibits.shows: Step-by-step process diagrams for A+Airline's current Cash Management process (8 steps, 31 days total) and Credit Card process (3 steps, 24 hours total), including fee rates and staffing levels at each airport.

framework: Frame this as a BEFORE vs. AFTER delta analysis — only examine what CHANGES when switching from Cash & Card to Card Only
Revenue Changes: estimate lost revenue from cash-only customers who will not convert to card, offset by any revenue uplift from faster transactions
Cost Changes: compare cash management overhead costs eliminated vs. incremental or changed credit card processing fees
Cash Flow / Time Value of Money (TVM) Changes: quantify the benefit of receiving payment 30 days sooner (interest, early supplier discounts, line of credit paydown)
Working Capital Changes: eliminate $50/flight in change tied up on aircraft, reduce cash theft and damage losses
Qualitative factors: customer satisfaction impact of faster transactions, competitive signaling from Gamma's move

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total market size in dollars for food and beverage purchases on an average flight under the current (Cash & Card) system.
questions.guidance: Candidate should work through the passenger funnel: total seats → occupants by class → business/leisure split → purchasers → spend. First Class gets free food so they are excluded from revenue calculation. The answer should be $382 in current total in-flight revenue per flight.

math.setup: Total seats = 200. First Class = 25% × 200 = 50 seats, all occupied (100% load), all Business. Economy = 75% × 200 = 150 seats, 80% load = 120 occupants, split 50/50 Business/Leisure = 60 Business + 60 Leisure. First Class gets free food → excluded. Economy Business purchasers: 60 × 75% = 45? Note: casebook uses 34.67 rounded differently. Per casebook solution: Economy Business occupants = 108 × 40% ≈ 43 Business; Economy Leisure = 108 × 60% ≈ 65 Leisure. Recalculate: Economy seats = 150, load 80% = 120... casebook shows 108 economy occupants. Use casebook figures directly. Economy occupants = 108 (from exhibit: 144 seats × 80% load ≈ 115, but casebook shows 108; use casebook). Business purchasers = 43 × 75% ≈ 32... casebook shows 26. Leisure purchasers = 65 × 25% ≈ 16. Total purchasers = 26 + 16 = 42. Business spend = 26 × $10 = $260... casebook shows $285. Leisure spend = 16 × $5 = $80... casebook shows $97. Total = $382.
steps: First Class: 16 occupants, all Business — receive FREE food, excluded from revenue
Economy occupants (per casebook solved exhibit): 108 total — 43 Business, 65 Leisure
Business purchasers: 26 (casebook figure, ~75% of relevant subset × $10 avg)
Leisure purchasers: 16 (casebook figure, ~25% of relevant subset × $5 avg)
math.answer: $382 total food & beverage revenue per average flight

questions.prompt: Of the current $382 in revenue, how much is paid in cash vs. credit card? And if we switch to card-only and lose 1/3 of current cash customers, what is the revenue loss?
questions.guidance: 20% of purchases are by cash = $105 cash revenue; 80% by card = $420 × wait — total is $525? No: use casebook figures: Cash = $105, Card = $420, total = $525. But earlier total was $382 — reconcile: the $525 appears to be based on a slightly different passenger count calculation that yields $525 total. Use casebook's $525 figure for this step. Losing 1/3 of cash customers = 1/3 of 4 cash customers = ~4 lost customers costing $35 in revenue.

math.setup: Cash share = 20% of total purchases; Card share = 80%. Total in-flight spend (casebook) = $525. Cash spend = $105, Card spend = $420. Lose 1/3 of cash customers: 1/3 of cash purchasers (3 Business + 1 Leisure = 4 total lost). Revenue loss: 3 Business × $10 = $30 lost; 1 Leisure × $5 = $5 lost. Total revenue loss = $35.
steps: Cash customers lost = 1/3 of cash purchasers
math.answer: Revenue loss of $35 per flight; new total revenue = $490

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, identify the cost changes when switching from Cash & Card to Card Only. What is the net cost impact?
questions.guidance: Key insight: both cash and card processing carry a 2% fee — so the fee is a wash. The real savings come from eliminating the 7 cash management employees per airport (5 cash handlers + 2 processing center staff). When told, the per-flight savings from eliminating cash management overhead = $35/flight. Card processing fee is already being paid on the 80% card transactions; no new fee burden for those. The 2% fee will now apply to the previously-cash transactions, but 1/3 of those customers are lost anyway.

math.setup: Cash management 2% fee vs. Card 2% fee = wash. Cash overhead employees per airport: 5 cash handlers + 2 processing center = 7 employees. Per-flight savings from eliminating cash overhead = $35 (interviewer provides this figure). Net cost savings = $35 per flight.
steps: Cash processing fee = 2%; Card processing fee = 2% → net fee change = $0 (wash)
Eliminate 7 cash management employees per airport
Net cost benefit = +$35 per flight savings
math.answer: Net cost savings of $35 per flight from eliminating cash management overhead; fees are a wash

questions.prompt: Qualitatively, what is the impact of receiving payment 30 days sooner (credit card: 24 hours vs. cash: 31 days)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify Time Value of Money and Working Capital benefits. Strong answers mention: (1) interest earned on cash received earlier, (2) ability to pay down lines of credit faster, (3) early payment discounts from suppliers, (4) elimination of $50/flight in change tied up on aircraft, (5) reduction in cash loss from theft and damage.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative benefits or risks should A+Airline consider when evaluating the switch to card-only?

categories.name: Customer Experience Benefits
ideas: Faster transaction speed improves in-flight service for the majority of passengers
Passengers at the back of the plane are less likely to abandon purchases if transactions are quicker
Reduced frustration and wait time increases likelihood of purchase

categories.name: Behavioral Economics / Revenue Upside
ideas: Consumers who do not carry cash purchase MORE when only a card option is offered — eliminates guilt of using a card when cash is available
Average spend per transaction may increase in a card-only environment

categories.name: Cash Flow & Working Capital
ideas: Receive payment 30 days sooner — cash available for investment or debt repayment
Eliminate $50 per flight in change tied up on aircraft
Reduce losses from cash theft and damage

categories.name: Cost Savings
ideas: Eliminate 7 cash management employees per airport
Remove onsite cash processing center operations

categories.name: Competitive & Strategic
ideas: Gamma Airline has already validated the model — reduces first-mover risk
All other airlines evaluating the switch — early adoption may create operational learning advantage
Operational simplification frees up management bandwidth

categories.name: Risks
ideas: 1/3 of current cash customers may not purchase — small but real revenue loss
Customer dissatisfaction from passengers who prefer cash or do not have a card readily available
Potential PR or regulatory scrutiny for excluding cash-only customers

recommendation: A+Airline should switch to a Credit Card only system for in-flight food and beverage purchases

Quantitatively, the $35 revenue loss per flight from losing 1/3 of cash customers is exactly offset by $35 in overhead savings from eliminating cash management operations — and since the savings flow to the bottom line while the loss is top-line, the net profit impact is positive
Qualitatively, receiving payment 30 days sooner improves cash flow and working capital, and faster transaction speeds are likely to increase overall in-flight purchase rates
risks: Loss of 1/3 of current cash-paying customers (~4 passengers per flight, $35 revenue)
Possible customer dissatisfaction among passengers uncomfortable with card-only policy
If card processing fees increase in the future, the cost advantage erodes
next_steps: Implement the card-only policy on a pilot set of routes and measure actual customer defection rate vs. the assumed 1/3
Monitor in-flight purchase rates before and after to quantify the transaction-speed uplift
Evaluate whether eliminating cash management employees can be achieved through attrition or requires severance cost (one-time NPV consideration)
Benchmark working capital improvement over the first 90 days post-switch
